title: Tears
hookLine: she writes of kinds of tears, from fear to love
tomorrow: how do crumbs scattered over the hills become one loaf?

cards: Some of the realest crying happens in a parked car, engine off, before going inside. Or in the shower, where nobody can tell. Afterward comes the urge to apologize, even to yourself, as if tears were a malfunction.
Catherine of Siena didn't treat them that way. In the Dialogue, God the Father talks with her about tears at length, kind by kind, and not one of them is dismissed as weakness.

teach.b: First, the ladder. In the Dialogue, tears come in kinds, and the kinds climb. At the bottom are tears of the world: grief over losses, with no hope looking past them.

Then tears of fear, from a soul that has seen its own wrong and is afraid. Then tears of someone beginning to love God, still partly for their own sake. Then tears of love, wept for God and for other people's good.
Second, what changes as you climb. Not the water. The reason.
The same eyes can weep from fear one year and from love another.

Third, the surprise: tears of fire. The Father says some people long to weep and can't, and their longing still counts; he calls it tears of fire, the Holy Spirit's own desire, burning where water won't come.
So nobody is shut out for being dry. Fourth, where that leaves a hard week.
Crying isn't a detour from prayer.
For Catherine it can be prayer, and the kind of tears tells you something about where love has reached. A grandmother crying because someone she loves is leaving isn't failing at anything.
Those may be tears of love: weeping for someone else's good.

how: Catholic tradition speaks of the gift of tears, weeping in prayer out of sorrow or love, and an old Mass prayer even asked for it; Catherine's Dialogue describes its kinds.

o: a sad hymn sung at funerals in Catherine's town
Catherine's kinds of weeping, from fear up to love
the drops of holy water sprinkled at a baptism

p: grief with no hope past it
a soul afraid of its own wrong
wept for God and others' good

s: Catholic saints treated crying as a sign of weak faith
in Catherine's Dialogue, the Father talks through tears kind by kind and dismisses none as weakness.
Catherine says someone who longs to weep and can't still has tears, of fire
the Holy Spirit's desire, burning where water won't come.
for Catherine, all tears are the same
they climb, from tears of fear to tears of love; the reason changes, not the water.

games.q: at a funeral, your cousin keeps apologizing for crying during the hymn. by Catherine's Dialogue, what could you say?
o: you're right; save it for later, somewhere private.
only tears of joy count with God, so try to smile.
no need to apologize; tears can be a prayer, and there's love in these.
games.why: Catherine climbs from tears of fear to tears of love, and treats none as a malfunction. tears for someone you loved belong in a church.

practice: Rest one hand over your heart and the other open on your knee. If something sad or tender is close to the surface, let it come, tears or no tears; if nothing comes, Catherine's Father would call that longing a fire, and it counts.
Breathe slowly under your hand until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Tears. Catherine's ladder of weeping, from tears of fear up to tears of love, with fire for those who can't cry.

orig.note: Latin for tears, as in the Salve Regina's in hac lacrimarum valle, in this valley of tears.

carryVoice: Your line: tears of love. The kind that cries for someone else's good. Go in peace.

sources.ref: The Dialogue, the treatise on tears (the kinds of tears; tears of fire)
Salve Regina ('in hac lacrimarum valle'), in games.original
